title: Why the bottom of the lake stays cold
teaches: Density and temperature, a lake's layers, Lake Washington's one winter mixing, and seiches
summary: **Heat barely moves through still water.** Conduction alone would take centuries to carry the summer's warmth 30 metres down, so a lake warms at depth only when its water is stirred.
**Fresh water is densest near 4 °C.** Warmer water is lighter and floats; below 4 °C water grows lighter again, so ice and near-freezing water float on top.
**The warmer the water, the more each degree changes its density.** Between 21 and 22 °C the change is about thirty times what it is between 4 and 5 °C, so a summer lake is layered firmly.
**A lake in summer has three layers.** A warm, wind-stirred top layer (the epilimnion), a thin layer where the temperature drops fast (the thermocline), and cold, still water below (the hypolimnion).
**The wind cannot lift heavy water through light.** A summer wind churns the top layer but not the cold water under it, which keeps last winter's temperature, about 7 °C in Lake Washington.
**Lake Washington mixes once a year, in early winter.** As the top cools to the bottom's temperature, the layers stop resisting, the wind stirs the whole lake, and it stays mixed until spring.
**A lake doesn't flip.** Its top layer cools, sinks and is stirred down until the lake is one body of water; nothing rolls over, and lakes that freeze mix twice, in spring and autumn.
**A seiche is a lake sloshing.** Wind piles water at one end; when it drops, the lake swings back and forth at its own natural period, set by its length and depth.
**The thermocline sloshes too, far more and far slower.** Wind tilts it the opposite way to the surface by hundreds of times as much, and it swings back and forth over days.

blocks.text: On a hot afternoon in August the top of Lake Washington is as warm as it gets all year, around 21 to 23 °C (70 to 73 °F), and swimmers at Madison Park and Matthews Beach stay in for an hour. At the bottom of the lake, 65 metres (214 feet) down at its deepest, the water is about 7 °C (45 °F), barely warmer than it was in February. It stays that cold all summer.[^level]

It has been sunny for three months, heat flows from warm to cold, and warm water lies right on top of cold water across the whole lake. The summer should be seeping down. Before reading on, try to think of what stops it.

Heat does creep through still water on its own, by **conduction**, each molecule jostling the next. The time it takes goes with the square of the distance: if heat soaks through a centimetre of still water in about ten minutes, then ten centimetres take a hundred times as long, about a day, and a metre about three months. Thirty metres would take some two hundred years.[^conduction] So conduction can be left out. Nearly all the heat that moves through a lake is carried by moving water: the wind stirring it, currents, and water sinking. The question becomes why the stirring stops partway down.

**Density** is how much a given volume of something weighs, here in grams per litre. A litre of fresh water at 20 °C weighs 998.2 grams; at 4 °C it weighs 1,000.0 grams. Like nearly everything, water expands as it warms, so warm water is lighter than cold and floats on it. Unlike nearly everything, fresh water stops shrinking near 4 °C and expands again as it cools further.[^four] Water at 1 °C floats on water at 4 °C, and ice, at 917 grams a litre, floats on all of it. Fresh water is densest near 4 °C.

blocks.caption: The weight of a litre of fresh water at each temperature, with Lake Washington's bottom and top in August marked. Ice, at 917 grams a litre, would be far off the bottom of the chart.

blocks.text: The curve has a second feature that matters as much as its peak: it gets steeper the warmer the water. From 4 to 5 °C, a litre gets lighter by less than a hundredth of a gram. From 21 to 22 °C, it gets lighter by about a fifth of a gram, around thirty times as much. Warm water on top of cold water is a strongly layered stack in summer, while in winter, with the whole lake between 6 and 8 °C, top and bottom differ hardly at all. Salt makes water heavier too, and lesson 12 adds it to the same idea for the Sound.

François-Alphonse Forel, a professor of medicine at Lausanne who lived at Morges on the shore of Lake Geneva, spent the 1870s to the 1900s measuring that lake in every way he could think of.[^forel] Among other things he and his colleagues lowered thermometers on lines from boats, month after month, and found what every deep lake in a mild climate shows in summer: the temperature does not fall smoothly with depth. It holds steady near the warm surface for a while, plunges within a few metres, and then stays cold and nearly uniform all the way down.

Limnologists, the scientists of lakes, name the three layers. The warm top layer, stirred by the wind, is the **epilimnion**; in Lake Washington in midsummer it is roughly the top ten metres. Below it, the thin layer where the temperature drops fast is the **thermocline**. Under that lies the cold, still **hypolimnion**, the bulk of the lake.

The wind stirs the top layer easily, because everything in it weighs the same. To stir the cold water up, the wind would have to lift heavy water through light water, which takes work, the way it takes work to lift a bucket. A summer breeze has enough to churn the top layer, and to drag its bottom edge a little deeper, but nowhere near enough to lift the layer below. The bottom water is left alone with last winter's temperature.

blocks.caption: Lake Washington through a year: the temperature at each depth (right) and a slice down the lake (left), coloured from cold to warm. Change the wind, and play the months. A model, calibrated roughly to the lake's measured temperatures: the surface follows the season, and the wind mixes down as far as its strength and the layers' difference in density allow.
blocks.task: Guess, then play the year until the whole lake mixes

blocks.title: Look it up
points: King County keeps moored buoys on Lake Washington and Lake Sammamish that measure the temperature at a string of depths, and its lake monitoring pages publish the profiles.
Look at one from August: the jump in temperature over a few metres is the thermocline. Look again in January, when the line runs straight down at one temperature.

blocks.text: In September the days shorten, the nights cool, and the top of the lake loses more heat each night than it gains each day. Cooled surface water is denser than the warmer water just under it, so it sinks, and the stirred top layer thickens, eating down into the thermocline. Autumn storms add their wind. Each degree the top loses shrinks the density difference that holds the layers apart, and because of the curve's shape, the last few degrees shrink it fastest.

By early winter the top has cooled to within a fraction of a degree of the bottom, the two weigh the same, and the next storm stirs Lake Washington from top to bottom. Through the winter the whole lake cools together, to about 6 or 7 °C, and the wind keeps all 65 metres moving. In spring the sun warms the top again. As soon as the top is a degree or two warmer than the bottom, the layers set and the wind can no longer reach down, and the bottom water is held near its late-winter temperature until the next December. That is the 7 °C in August.

A lake that mixes top to bottom once a year is **monomictic**. Lake Washington is a warm monomictic lake: its top never cools below 4 °C, so it never layers the other way in winter and it does not freeze over.[^mictic] Mixing also carries oxygen from the air down to the bottom water, which matters a great deal to what lives there; a later course on the life in the water picks that up.

A lake in a colder place, such as a mountain lake that freezes each winter, mixes twice. It mixes in autumn as its top cools to 4 °C, then layers upside down under the ice, with water near 0 °C, the lightest, just under the ice and 4 °C water on the bottom. In spring, once the ice melts and the top warms to 4 °C, it mixes again before the summer layers form. This twice-mixed lake is the one most textbooks draw.

blocks.title: Misconception: the lake flips over
points: Books often say a lake "turns over" in autumn, and diagrams show the bottom water rising to the top as if the lake rolled over like a pancake.
Nothing rolls over. The top layer cools, sinks and is stirred deeper, until the lake is one body of water at one temperature and the wind mixes all of it.
Limnologists still call this the turnover; the word describes the result, a lake mixed through, not a flip.

blocks.text: Forel was also curious about something people on Lake Geneva had noticed for centuries. On calm days the water at Geneva, at the narrow western end of the lake, would rise and fall by a few centimetres, sometimes much more, over an hour or so, with no wind and no tide to explain it. Locals called it a **seiche**. Forel set up recording gauges at several places around the lake and showed that the whole lake was sloshing from end to end, like water in a bathtub, with one end high while the other was low, and a swing that took a little over an hour.

Wind starts it. A steady wind blowing along a lake drags the surface water with it and piles it up at the downwind end, a little like a breath piling water at one end of a bath. When the wind drops, the piled water runs back, overshoots, and runs back again. The lake rocks about its middle, which barely moves, while the ends swing up and down. A wave that runs back and forth between two ends in this way, with places that stay still and places that swing, is a **standing wave**. Its period is the time a long wave takes to run the length of the lake and back. Such a wave goes faster in deeper water, about 18 metres a second in water as deep as Lake Washington's average of 33 metres, so the lake, about 35 kilometres (22 miles) long, sloshes once an hour or so; lesson 7 explains why depth sets the speed.[^quake]

The same wind does something larger and slower out of sight. Pushing the warm top layer to the downwind end piles warm water up there, so the thermocline sinks at that end and rises at the upwind end. Because the warm and cold layers differ in density by only about two parts in a thousand, it takes very little push to tilt the boundary between them, and its tilt is hundreds of times the surface's. After a strong wind that blows along the lake for a day, the thermocline at the upwind end can rise all the way to the surface, and swimmers there find the lake suddenly cold.

blocks.caption: A summer lake cut along its length, with a warm layer over cold. Set the wind that has blown along it for a day, then drop it and play the hours after. The surface's tilt is drawn 200 times larger than it is; the thermocline's is drawn true to the depth. A model of a box 35 km long and 33 m deep, with a warm layer 10 m thick.
blocks.task: Guess, then watch the thermocline swing back

blocks.text: When the wind drops, the thermocline sloshes too, as an **internal seiche**, a standing wave on the boundary between the layers. With so little difference in weight to pull it back, it swings slowly: in a lake the size of Lake Washington, about once every two days, while the surface above has long since settled. Hold on to the seiche. A bay or a sound has its own sloshing period, and lesson 10 finds Puget Sound's close enough to the tide's to make Olympia's tide twice Port Townsend's.

blocks.caption: Six questions on lakes
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: In August the bottom of Lake Washington is about 7 °C while the top is above 20 °C. Which explanation is best?
choices: The light, warm top layer lies on heavy, cold water, and the wind cannot lift heavy water through light, so the bottom keeps last winter's temperature
Cold springs on the lake floor keep feeding fresh cold water into the bottom of the lake all summer
Sunlight cannot reach below a few metres, and the water stays cold wherever the sun does not shine directly on it
items.why: Heat moves through a lake mainly by stirring, and stable layers stop the stirring. Conduction alone would take centuries to carry heat 30 metres down, so the bottom water keeps the temperature it had when the lake last mixed.

items.ask: At about what temperature is fresh water densest?
items.why: Water shrinks as it cools down to about 4 °C and then expands again, so water near freezing and ice float on 4 °C water.

items.ask: Why does a summer lake resist mixing far more strongly than the same lake does in winter?
choices: Water's density changes much more per degree when it is warm, so warm water over cold differs a lot in weight
Winter winds are always several times stronger than summer winds on lakes
The lake holds more water in winter, so it is easier to stir
items.why: The density curve is steep at warm temperatures and nearly flat near 4 °C. A summer lake's layers differ a lot in weight; a winter lake's hardly at all.

items.ask: When does Lake Washington mix from top to bottom, and how often?
choices: Once a year, when its top cools to the bottom's temperature in early winter, and it stays mixed until spring
Twice a year, in spring and autumn, when the lake flips over
Every night in summer, when the air cools the surface below the bottom's temperature
items.why: Lake Washington is warm monomictic: its top never cools below 4 °C and it never freezes, so it mixes once, in early winter, and stays mixed all winter.

items.ask: Which describes a lake's autumn turnover best?
choices: The cooling top layer sinks and is stirred ever deeper until the whole lake is one temperature and the wind mixes it all
The bottom water warms up, becomes lighter and rises, while the top water drops to the bottom in one quick flip
Ice forming on the surface pushes the top water down and squeezes the bottom water up
items.why: Nothing flips. The top cools and sinks, the stirred layer deepens, and once top and bottom weigh the same the wind mixes the lake through.

items.ask: A steady wind blows along a layered lake for a day. What happens at the upwind end?
choices: The surface drops a little and the thermocline rises a lot, sometimes bringing cold water to the surface
The surface rises a lot and the thermocline sinks a little
The surface drops and the thermocline sinks with it by the same amount
items.why: The wind pushes the warm top layer downwind. The surface tilts up toward the downwind end by centimetres or less; the thermocline tilts the opposite way by metres, because the two layers differ so little in weight.

level.title: A lowered lake
level.text: The lake's surface itself was lowered by about 2.7 metres (nearly 9 feet) in 1916, when the ship canal opened; the Seattle branch (S2) tells that story.

conduction.title: How slow conduction is
conduction.text: Heat spreads through still water with a diffusivity of about 0.14 square millimetres a second. The time to spread a distance L is roughly L² divided by that: about 12 minutes for a centimetre, 80 days for a metre, and 200 years for 30 metres. Moving water carries heat thousands of times faster.

four.title: Why 4 °C
four.text: Water molecules cling to each other by hydrogen bonds, which prefer an open, spacious arrangement, the one locked in place in ice. Below about 4 °C more and more molecules fall into loose versions of that open arrangement, and the water expands even as it cools. Above 4 °C ordinary expansion with heat wins. Salt water behaves differently: sea water gets denser all the way down to freezing, which lesson 12 needs.

forel.title: Forel
forel.text: François-Alphonse Forel (1841 to 1912) wrote his findings into *Le Léman*, three volumes published from 1892 to 1904, and named the science of lakes **limnology**. His colour scale, a row of numbered tubes of tinted liquid to hold against a lake, is still used to describe the colour of natural waters.

mictic.title: Mixing types
mictic.text: Limnologists sort lakes by how often they mix top to bottom: **monomictic** once a year, **dimictic** twice (spring and autumn, in lakes that freeze), **polymictic** many times (shallow lakes the wind can stir to the bottom in any season), and **meromictic** never, where a dense, often salty bottom layer is never stirred.

quake.title: Seiches from earthquakes
quake.text: Lakes can be set sloshing by distant earthquakes too. The great Alaska earthquake of March 1964 and the Denali earthquake of November 2002 set Lake Union swinging; in 2002 houseboats there broke moorings and pipes, more than 2,000 kilometres from the fault.
